chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Muhammad ibn Isma'il said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the covering (qina') of free women by the eunuchs. He said: 'They used to enter upon the daughters of Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and they would not cover themselves. Therefore, the meaning in this report is a form of taqiyyah (dissimulation/prudence), and acting upon the first report is more preferable and more cautious in religion.' And in another report, when he was asked about this issue, he said: 'Restrain yourself from this.' It was known from his restraining himself from answering that it was for a form of taqiyyah; he did not say what he had in mind regarding that, due to the usage of the sultans of the time of that.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّة: Dissimulation or prudence in concealing truth

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on women covering their heads (qina') in the presence of eunuchs according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records that Imam al-Rida (AS) clarified the practice of free women of the Ahl al-Bayt not wearing head coverings (*qina'*) when eunuchs entered, attributing this to *taqiyyah* (dissimulation) rather than a permanent ruling. This distinction highlights the scholarly principle of differentiating between temporary precautionary measures and definitive legal rulings, especially under the political pressure of the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs. The Imam’s silence in other instances further illustrates how *taqiyyah* was employed to conceal specific jurisprudential details from the ruling authorities.
